articles.title: IFFJK marks new chapter in region's storied romance with silver screen: Omar Abdullah
articles.description:
Srinagar, Sep 7 (PTI): Jammu and Kashmir's cinematic appeal goes far beyond its scenic vistas, into the very cultural ethos of 'Kashmiriyat', Chief Minister Omar Abdullah said on Monday, asserting that the International Film Festival marks a new chapter in the region's storied romance with the silver screen.

Addressing the inaugural International Film Festival of Jammu and Kashmir (IFFJK) at the Kashmir International Conference Centre here, Abdullah made a passionate pitch to national and international filmmakers to carry a piece of Jammu and Kashmir in their hearts, asserting the Union territory was open, safe, vibrant, and eager to once again welcome film crews.

Abdullah urged domestic and overseas filmmakers, and delegates attending the opening ceremony of the four-day film festival, to become ambassadors for the Union territory. "To our foreign and national delegates: carry a piece of Jammu and Kashmir back in your hearts. Tell your fellow filmmakers that Jammu and Kashmir is open, safe, vibrant, and eager to welcome your crews." The chief minister's remarks came amid ongoing government efforts to re-establish Jammu and Kashmir as a premier destination for film production, rekindling a historic romance with cinema that once made the Valley a staple on Indian silver screens.

Addressing the youth, Abdullah urged them to harness the festival's momentum to tell their own stories on the global stage. "Let these four days inspire you. Your stories matter. Your voices matter. The world is listening," he said.

Highlighting cinema's power to transcend cultural and geopolitical divides, he said it is an universal language that knows no borders, requires no translation, and reminds us of our shared humanity, urging filmmakers to "seek out stories" of Jammu and Kashmir.

"For generations, poets have celebrated Kashmir as 'Jannat-e-Firdous' (paradise on earth). It is the world's most breathtaking natural canvas, a place where reality itself feels lit by a cinematographer's touch," he said.

The chief minister said the festival, that brings together filmmakers from more than 40 countries and showcases over 130 films, posits Jammu and Kashmir as a "creative sanctuary, a home for global storytellers, and a voice ready to speak to the world".

Abdullah revisited Kashmir's deep-rooted connection to cinema, saying it has provided the visual backdrop for some of the most iconic moments in film history. "In the golden era of Indian cinema, to fall in love on screen meant falling in love in Kashmir," he mused.

Pointing to yesteryear's blockbusters shot in Kashmir, he referred iconic moments such as Shammi Kapoor's snow-laden shouts in 'Junglee', Sharmila Tagore on Dal Lake in 'Kashmir Ki Kali', and Yash Chopra's romance epics 'Kabhi Kabhie' and 'Silsila'.

He also acknowledged modern cinema's shift toward more layered storytelling in projects like Vidhu Vinod Chopra's 'Mission Kashmir', Vishal Bhardwaj's 'Haider', and Imtiaz Ali's 'Rockstar' and 'Highway'.

However, the chief minister asserted that cinema is more than landscapes. "The true beauty of Jammu and Kashmir lies in its soul, its cultural ethos built on Kashmiriyat, warmth, hospitality, and a rich artistic tradition," he said.

Kashmir has always been a land of storytellers, he said. "Long before cameras arrived, our heritage was woven through sound, craft, and oral traditions." Emphasising that nostalgia alone cannot build an industry, the chief minister said to welcome the future of filmmaking, Jammu and Kashmir must build an ecosystem that nurtures it.

"That is precisely what we are doing under our comprehensive Jammu and Kashmir Film Policy. We aim to transform the Union territory from a beautiful location into one of the most filmmaker-friendly destinations," he said, pointing to the single-window clearance system for film and location permits and security arrangements.

He announced that the government is planning to invest meaningfully in modern post-production facilities, equipment banks, film studios, and film education institutes to ensure complete end-to-end production ecosystems. "We are treating cinema not merely as entertainment, but as an industry-- one that generates employment, nurtures young talent, and bridges global cultures." Former chief minister Farooq Abdullah, who attended the ceremony, was seen enthusiastically clapping, tapping his feet and humming tunes while various artists including playback singer Rani Hazarika enthralled the audience.

The venue on the banks of the Dal Lake came alive with sound beats and light. "We don't usually have such events in Kashmir. This is perhaps for the first time that we got to witness such a huge event. I thoroughly enjoyed it and will remember it for a long time," Yawar Ahmad, a resident of the uptown area of the city here, said. PTI SSB ARB ARB

articles.title: J-K film festival will open new opportunities, showcase Kashmir's bond with Indian cinema: Minister
articles.description:
Srinagar, Sept 7 (PTI): Union minister Jitendra Singh on Monday expressed hope that the International Film Festival of Jammu and Kashmir (IFFJK) will not only add to the vibrant cultural landscape of the Union territory but also open new opportunities for the youth.

Singh, addressing the inauguration ceremony of the maiden IFFJK here, said the event sends a strong message to the world that cinema is just as popular in Jammu and Kashmir as it is across the country.

The minister lauded the organisers of the film festival, asserting that the prevailing normalcy in the Union territory has enabled cultural ventures of this scale.

"We are grateful to Prime Minister Narendra Modi that the situation here is becoming favourable, and returning to normal to an extent that we are able to successfully organise this programme here," he said, also expressing his gratitude towards the state government and Chief Minister Omar Abdullah.

Singh said this event is heartwarming as he had witnessed the era when cinema halls here started closing down one after the other. "A long period of about 20-25 years passed when we were deprived of cinema.

"Yet, this region has had an inseparable relationship with Indian cinema. We have seen the days when film shootings took place in every street-corner, garden and scenic vistas of Kashmir. Hotels and houseboats used to be bustling with guests from the film industry," he said.

Taking a trip down memory lane, the Union minister recalled the filming of a song from the Amitabh Bachchan-starrer "Kabhi Kabhie" in the Valley.

"I still remember the filming of 'Kabhi Kabhie' here. It featured a song -- this beautiful lyric by Sahir Ludhianvi, 'Main pal do pal ka shayar hoon'. The scene shows Amitabh Bachchan singing the song on a stage at a college programme. The audience in the sequence featured actual students from the Government College for Women, Srinagar," he said.

Singh said he considers the film festival a great platform for the local artists.

"Older generations will recall that during the 1950s and 1960s, many of our finest artists hailed from Kashmir. Among top actors, Raaj Kumar, Jeevan, Sapru, and Om Prakash were all from Kashmir.

"Rajendra Singh Bedi didn't belong to Kashmir, but he served as the station director for Jammu Radio Station and later wrote dialogues for films like Devdas. Balraj Sahni was from Punjab, but he visited Kashmir extensively. Vidhu Vinod Chopra is our friend and college senior -- he also belongs here," he said.

The Union minister asserted that while Kashmir has enriched Bollywood, the film industry has, in turn, enriched the Valley. PTI MIJ ARB ARB
